title: Propensity Score Matching Balances Covariates
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: Propensity score matching pairs treated and control units with similar probabilities of treatment given covariates to reduce confounding.
short: Match people with similar treatment chances.
long: Match people with similar treatment chances. Balance diagnostics check whether matching succeeded.
proof: Conditional on the propensity score, treatment is independent of covariates under ignorability.
consequence: A common observational causal estimator.

title: Double Machine Learning Debiases Treatment Effects
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: Double machine learning uses cross-fitted nuisance estimates and orthogonal scores so that regularization errors do not bias the treatment-effect estimate.
short: Cross-fit nuisances to remove first-order bias.
long: Cross-fit nuisances to remove first-order bias. Neyman orthogonality makes the estimator robust to slow nuisance learning.
proof: Cross-fitting independentizes nuisance estimates from the evaluation sample and orthogonality cancels first-order errors.
consequence: Brings flexible ML into valid causal inference.

title: Causal Forests Estimate Heterogeneous Effects
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: Causal forests use tree ensembles with honest splitting to estimate how treatment effects vary across covariates.
short: Trees that estimate local treatment effects.
long: Trees that estimate local treatment effects. Honest splitting uses separate data for tree structure and effect estimation.
proof: Local randomized or residualized comparisons are averaged over trees to produce conditional effect estimates.
consequence: Supports personalized treatment-effect estimation.

title: Invariant Risk Minimization Seeks Stable Predictors
subject: Machine Learning Theory
statement: Invariant risk minimization aims to learn representations whose optimal classifier is the same across training environments, encouraging out-of-distribution generalization.
short: Seek features that work the same in every environment.
long: Seek features that work the same in every environment. The penalty encourages the invariance of the optimal linear predictor.
proof: Requiring a shared optimal classifier across environments discourages reliance on environment-specific correlations.
consequence: A theoretical approach to causal feature learning.

title: Invariant Risk Minimization Can Fail Empirically
subject: Machine Learning Theory
statement: Empirically, invariant risk minimization can fail on nonlinear or insufficiently varied environments, sometimes learning degenerate invariant solutions.
short: Invariance penalties do not always deliver robustness.
long: Invariance penalties do not always deliver robustness. Careful environment design and diagnostics matter.
proof: Empirical: constructed nonlinear tasks show IRM converging to trivial constant classifiers.
consequence: Highlights gaps between invariance theory and practice.

title: Truncated Factorization Gives Interventional Distributions
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: In a causal Bayesian network, the distribution after intervening on a set of variables factors with the structural equations for the intervened variables replaced by point masses.
latex: P(y\mid do(x))=\prod_{i\notin X}P(x_i\mid x_{\mathrm{pa}(i)})\ \mathbf{1}[x_i=\hat{x}_i\ \mathrm{for}\ i\in X]
short: Cut incoming edges for intervened nodes.
long: Cut incoming edges for intervened nodes. This is the truncated factorization formula.
proof: The intervention removes the parents of each manipulated variable, so those factors vanish from the joint.
consequence: Connects graph structure to intervention calculations.

title: Counterfactual Fairness Requires a Causal Model
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: Counterfactual fairness requires a decision to be unchanged in a counterfactual world where only the protected attribute is altered, which needs a causal model to define.
short: Fairness can be defined by counterfactual invariance.
long: Fairness can be defined by counterfactual invariance. Without causal assumptions the counterfactual is not identifiable.
proof: Changing a protected attribute while holding other variables fixed requires specifying which descendants change.
consequence: Makes causal assumptions explicit in fairness analysis.

title: Collider Conditioning Can Reverse Associations
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: Conditioning on a common effect of two variables can create a spurious association between them, potentially reversing the sign of an estimated effect.
latex: X\perp Y,\ \mathrm{but}\ X\not\perp Y\mid C,\ C\leftarrow X,\ C\leftarrow Y
short: Selecting on a common effect creates false dependence.
long: Selecting on a common effect creates false dependence. This is Berkson's paradox or collider bias.
proof: Conditioning on a collider opens a path between its parents in the graphical criterion.
consequence: Warns against indiscriminate covariate adjustment.

title: Federated Averaging Aggregates Local Updates
subject: Machine Learning
statement: Federated averaging trains locally on each client for several steps and averages the resulting model updates on a server.
short: Train locally, average globally.
long: Train locally, average globally. Weighting by client sample size is the standard aggregation rule.
proof: Local SGD steps approximate a global step; averaging combines the clients' estimates.
consequence: The foundational algorithm of federated learning.

title: Federated Rounds Dominate Communication Cost
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: In federated learning the bottleneck is often the repeated exchange of model updates between server and clients, not local computation.
short: Sending models costs more than training locally.
long: Sending models costs more than training locally. Compression and fewer local steps trade accuracy for less communication.
proof: Each round transmits a full model to selected clients and back, which dominates when models are large.
consequence: Drives research on communication-efficient federated algorithms.

title: Non-IID Clients Slow Federated Convergence Empirically
subject: Machine Learning
statement: Empirically, heterogeneous client data distributions make local updates diverge and slow or destabilize federated convergence.
short: Different clients pull the model in different directions.
long: Different clients pull the model in different directions. Personalization and proximal terms mitigate client drift.
proof: Empirical: non-IID partitions produce lower accuracy and more client drift than shuffled IID partitions.
consequence: Client heterogeneity is a central federated challenge.

title: Secure Aggregation Hides Individual Updates
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: Secure aggregation protocols let a server recover only the sum of client updates without seeing any individual update.
short: The server sees only the aggregate.
long: The server sees only the aggregate. Pairwise masks cancel when updates are summed.
proof: Cryptographic masks are chosen so that each client's mask cancels with others in the aggregate.
consequence: Reduces privacy leakage from update inspection.

title: DP-SGD Clips Gradients and Adds Noise
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: Differentially private SGD clips each example's gradient to a fixed norm and adds calibrated Gaussian noise to the averaged gradient.
short: Clip per-example influence, then add noise.
long: Clip per-example influence, then add noise. Privacy accounting tracks the budget across training steps.
proof: Bounding sensitivity by C and adding noise proportional to C gives differential privacy by the Gaussian mechanism.
consequence: The standard private deep-learning optimizer.

title: Privacy Loss Composes Across Queries
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: Under sequential composition, the privacy parameters of multiple mechanisms applied to the same data add.
short: Each query spends part of the privacy budget.
long: Each query spends part of the privacy budget. Advanced composition can give tighter bounds for many queries.
proof: The failure probability of a chain of private mechanisms is bounded by the sum of individual bounds.
consequence: Requires budget accounting for long training runs.

title: Renyi Differential Privacy Simplifies Accounting
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: Renyi differential privacy measures privacy loss with Renyi divergences and offers tight composition for repeated Gaussian mechanisms.
short: A divergence-based budget that composes cleanly.
long: A divergence-based budget that composes cleanly. It can be converted back to standard differential privacy guarantees.
proof: Renyi divergences compose additively under product mechanisms, simplifying the analysis of many steps.
consequence: Underlies modern privacy accounting for DP-SGD.

title: Membership Inference Exploits Confidence Gaps
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: Membership inference attacks guess whether a record was in training by exploiting higher confidence or lower loss on memorized examples.
short: Trained-on examples often look more familiar.
long: Trained-on examples often look more familiar. Calibration and regularization can reduce the signal.
proof: Empirical: members have systematically lower loss than comparable nonmembers.
consequence: Reveals privacy leakage from model outputs.

title: Model Inversion Reconstructs Class Representatives
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: Model inversion attacks optimize an input to maximize a model's confidence for a target class, recovering class-representative data.
short: Optimize an input that looks like a target class.
long: Optimize an input that looks like a target class. Successful reconstruction leaks information about training classes.
proof: Gradient ascent on class probability produces inputs resembling the learned class prototype.
consequence: Shows privacy risk from exposed model predictions.

title: Training Data Can Be Extracted from Language Models Empirically
subject: AI Safety & Interpretability
statement: Empirically, language models can be made to reproduce verbatim sequences from their training data, including sensitive text.
short: Models sometimes recite their training data.
long: Models sometimes recite their training data. Extraction attacks use tailored prompts and likelihood searches.
proof: Empirical: extraction studies recover memorized documents from deployed language models.
consequence: Motivates data sanitization and privacy-preserving training.

title: Homomorphic Encryption Allows Computing on Ciphertexts
subject: Probabilistic AI
statement: Homomorphic encryption supports computing a function on encrypted data so that decrypting the result matches computing the function on plaintext.
short: Compute without decrypting the data.
long: Compute without decrypting the data. Fully homomorphic schemes support arbitrary circuits with bootstrapping.
proof: The encryption scheme provides operations whose ciphertext results decrypt to the corresponding plaintext operations.
consequence: Enables privacy-preserving inference on untrusted servers.

title: Federated Learning Trades Accuracy for Privacy Empirically
subject: Machine Learning
statement: Empirically, adding differential privacy to federated training lowers utility, with stronger privacy budgets causing larger accuracy losses.
short: Stronger privacy usually costs accuracy.
long: Stronger privacy usually costs accuracy. The trade-off depends on model size, client count and clipping settings.
proof: Empirical: federated experiments sweep the privacy budget and observe monotone accuracy changes.
consequence: Guides realistic privacy-utility targets.

title: Watermarks Embed Statistical Signals in Generations
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: A watermark deliberately biases generated output so that a statistical test can later identify it as model-generated.
short: Hide a detectable signature in the output.
long: Hide a detectable signature in the output. Watermarks may modify tokens, images or continuous signals.
proof: The embedding rule changes the output distribution in a known way that a detector tests for.
consequence: Supports provenance and misuse tracking.

title: Green List Watermarks Bias Token Sampling
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Token-level watermarking partitions the vocabulary into a green list and red list based on prior tokens and slightly favors green-list sampling.
short: Nudge sampling toward a key-dependent word list.
long: Nudge sampling toward a key-dependent word list. The key determines the partition, so unauthorized parties cannot forge the pattern.
proof: Biasing logits by a constant delta raises green-list probability while keeping sampling nearly lossless.
consequence: A practical watermark for language-model output.

title: Watermark Detection Uses Statistical Tests
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: A watermark detector counts green-list tokens and tests whether the count exceeds what chance sampling would produce.
short: Count signature tokens and compute a z-score.
long: Count signature tokens and compute a z-score. Longer texts give higher detection power.
proof: Under the null, green-list counts follow a binomial distribution with probability equal to the green-list fraction.
consequence: Gives a principled false-positive rate for detection.

title: Watermarks Degrade under Paraphrasing Empirically
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Empirically, paraphrasing or heavy editing can remove statistical watermarks from generated text.
short: Rewriting can wash out the signature.
long: Rewriting can wash out the signature. Robust watermarks are an active area of research.
proof: Empirical: detector scores drop after paraphrasing attacks while text meaning is preserved.
consequence: Limits watermark reliability in adversarial settings.

title: AI-Text Detectors Generalize Poorly Empirically
subject: AI Systems & Evaluation
statement: Empirically, AI-generated-text detectors trained on one model or domain often fail on unseen generators and domains.
short: Detectors overfit to the generator they saw.
long: Detectors overfit to the generator they saw. Performance also drops on edited or translated text.
proof: Empirical: cross-model and cross-domain evaluations show large accuracy drops.
consequence: Detectors should not be treated as definitive evidence.
